gold_rationale: Paper A is an offensive contribution that backdoors the retriever (corpus/embedding side) to induce prompt-injection behavior in RAG and reports attack success rate, while Paper B is a defensive contribution that leverages attack-style techniques (likely prompt-level perturbation or known-answer probing) to detect or neutralize prompt injection. The two occupy opposite roles in the attack-defense pipeline with mismatched intervention points, threat-model assumptions, and metric targets, and Paper B may not even be RAG-specific. As in P08/P09, direct leaderboard ranking is structurally inappropriate.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Recast both inside a shared attack-defense harness with a fixed retriever, generator, corpus, and target-query set; instantiate Paper A's backdoored-retriever attack (with matched trigger budget and poisoning rate) as the adversary and evaluate Paper B's defense alongside baselines such as paraphrase filtering, perplexity screening, and RobustRAG; report a joint suite of attack success rate, clean accuracy, robust/certified accuracy, and abstention rate under a single declared threat model.

gold_rationale: Both papers attack RAG via adversarial content placed in the retrieval corpus, so the broad failure family (integrity violation through retrieved text) and the corpus-side intervention surface partially align. However, the threat models diverge sharply: ADMIT injects optimized few-shot poisoned passages to flip a fact-checking verdict (content corruption with task-specific veracity labels), while Hidden-in-Plain-Text studies indirect prompt injection from social-web text aiming to hijack instruction-following in general RAG. Different attacker goals, different downstream tasks (fact verification vs open RAG), and different success metrics (verdict flip rate vs IPI execution/compliance) prevent direct ranking. Also, paper A is an attack method, paper B is a benchmark.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Build a unified adversarial-RAG harness that fixes retriever, generator, and corpus, then instantiates both attack families (knowledge poisoning and indirect prompt injection) on a shared task suite covering both fact-checking and open-domain RAG, with a common metric bundle (attack success rate, clean-task accuracy, abstention) under matched insertion budgets. Reciprocally, the HiPT benchmark would need a fact-checking slice, and ADMIT would need to be reformulated to expose IPI-style payloads to be ranked on it.

gold_rationale: Both papers occupy the RAG corpus-poisoning threat space, so the failure type broadly aligns. However, ProGRank is a defender contribution intervening at reranking with metrics on clean and robust accuracy plus a filter/rerank action policy, while Paper B is a vulnerability analysis whose role is to characterize or demonstrate attacks (likely reporting attack success rate without a defender action). Paper B's explicit scoping to knowledge-intensive application domains also signals a likely evidence-distribution mismatch with ProGRank's general dense-retriever benchmarks. Direct leaderboard ranking is structurally inappropriate due to the attack-vs-defense role asymmetry.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Recast as a shared attack-defense harness: fix retriever, generator, corpus, and target-query set on a knowledge-intensive domain that both works can support; instantiate Paper B's attack(s) with matched insertion budgets against ProGRank alongside baseline defenses; jointly report attack success rate, clean accuracy, robust accuracy, abstention rate, and reranking latency under adaptive-adversary variants aware of probe-gradient scoring.

gold_rationale: Paper A is a defensive contribution that detects embedded instructions in retrieved context to mitigate indirect prompt injection in standard text RAG, while Paper B is an offensive contribution that crafts minimal-word knowledge poisoning to distort graph-based RAG. The roles are asymmetric (defense vs attack), the RAG substrates differ (text vs knowledge graph), the failure modes diverge (executable instruction smuggling vs factual graph distortion), and the headline metrics are opposed (detection/defense success vs attack success rate). No substitutable head-to-head ranking is possible.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Reframe inside a shared attack-defense harness on a common RAG architecture: fix retriever, generator, and corpus/graph; instantiate Paper B's poisoning (and an indirect-prompt-injection adversary) as attackers with matched insertion budgets; evaluate Paper A's instruction detector alongside other defenses on both text-RAG and graph-RAG; jointly report attack success rate, detection precision/recall, clean accuracy, and abstention under aligned threat models.

gold_rationale: Paper A is a training-free RAG method that uses uncertainty to trigger retrieval and routes queries through dual paths, primarily optimizing answer quality and retrieval necessity on standard QA. Paper B is an evaluation library specifically targeting out-of-knowledge-base robustness, where the central concern is whether the system correctly abstains when the KB lacks the answer. The method-vs-benchmark asymmetry plus divergent failure framing (when-to-retrieve vs when-to-abstain) prevents direct leaderboard ranking, though uncertainty-aware behavior provides a conceptual bridge that makes the pair more than unrelated.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Paper A's uncertainty-triggered dual-path framework on Paper B's KnowOrNot OOKB testbeds with matched LLM backbones, reporting abstention/refusal accuracy alongside answer correctness under a unified action-policy contract. Symmetrically, evaluate the baselines profiled by Paper B on Paper A's in-KB ODQA tasks so both in-KB efficiency and OOKB abstention are measured on a shared protocol.

gold_rationale: Both papers sit in the adaptive-retrieval family that asks when a search-augmented LLM should invoke retrieval versus rely on parametric knowledge, so the failure mode (unnecessary or harmful retrieval) and evidence assumption (parametric knowledge sometimes suffices) overlap. However, Paper A appears diagnostic, characterizing over-searching as a phenomenon in search-augmented LLMs, while QuCo-RAG is a methodological intervention that gates retrieval via pre-training-corpus uncertainty estimates. Action policies diverge (problem identification vs. retrieve/skip gating) and likely metrics differ (over-search rate vs. accuracy plus retrieval-frequency tradeoff), preventing direct leaderboard ranking.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix the same base LLM, retriever, and QA suite; run QuCo-RAG alongside naive always-retrieve and never-retrieve baselines on the over-searching diagnostic protocol from Paper A; jointly report over-search rate, retrieval frequency, and end-task accuracy under a shared retrieve-vs-abstain action contract so the method can be scored against the diagnosed pathology.

gold_rationale: Both works address the shared concern of when a RAG system should trust retrieved evidence versus abstain or fall back on parametric knowledge, so the underlying failure mode (miscalibrated grounding) overlaps. However, the evidence modality diverges fundamentally: Paper A operates over knowledge-graph triples with a causality-aware calibration mechanism (likely inference-time scoring), while Paper B works on textual contextual evidence and intervenes via RL fine-tuning of the generator with an explicit abstention action. The intervention points and action policies are not directly substitutable on a common leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix a shared evidence modality (either KG-grounded or text-grounded, or a harness that supports both) and a common abstention-aware metric bundle covering answer correctness, abstention/rejection rate, and calibration error. Evaluate both the calibration scorer and the RL-trained policy on matched query sets with controlled retrieval-quality variation, under a single declared answer-versus-abstain action contract.

gold_rationale: Both works target trustworthy RAG and likely share answer correctness as a base metric, but they occupy different roles. Paper A is a method intervention that calibrates the generator so confidence supports downstream decisions, with calibration metrics such as ECE or Brier as headline targets. Paper B is a diagnostic lens that stratifies RAG behavior by whether retrieved context is sufficient to answer, characterizing hallucination patterns rather than proposing a calibration training procedure. The failure framings (miscalibration vs context insufficiency) overlap conceptually but are not directly rankable.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Paper A's calibration-oriented RAG on Paper B's sufficient vs insufficient context partition over a shared QA benchmark with fixed retriever and generator, reporting ECE, Brier, accuracy, and abstention rate per slice. Symmetrically apply Paper B's sufficiency classifier to Paper A's evaluation to test whether calibration gains concentrate on the insufficient-context slice and to align action policies (answer vs abstain).

gold_rationale: Both works share the broad theme of LLM robustness to distractors, but the distractor artifact differs fundamentally: PrismRAG targets retrieved distractor passages inside a RAG pipeline and intervenes via a training method to improve answer factuality, while DistractionIF examines distractor instructions in the prompt and is a diagnostic study reporting an inverse scaling law in instruction-following. The evaluation harnesses (RAG factuality vs instruction-following accuracy), intervention modes (method vs diagnostic), and action policies (answer with retrieved evidence vs comply with target instruction) do not align, so a direct leaderboard ranking is not warranted, though they share a distraction-robustness frame.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix shared LLM backbones and construct a unified distractor harness that evaluates both regimes — retrieved distractor passages and injected distractor instructions — with matched distractor budgets and difficulty. Apply PrismRAG's training intervention to instruction-following settings and inject DistractionIF-style distractor instructions into RAG prompts, then report per-regime accuracy plus a scaling-law slice across model sizes so method gains and inverse-scaling effects can be jointly measured.

gold_rationale: Both works address how retrieved passages degrade RAG generation quality and likely share answer-correctness metrics on overlapping QA benchmarks, so they sit in the same problem family. However, Paper A targets position sensitivity (lost-in-the-middle ordering bias) with a generator-side architectural intervention that fuses KV caches in parallel to enforce position invariance, while Paper B targets distractor-passage selection with a retriever-side training intervention that learns to avoid distraction-inducing contexts. The failure modes (position bias vs content distraction) and intervention points (generator KV fusion vs retriever learning) are orthogonal, making any direct leaderboard ranking misleading.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix a shared retriever-generator stack and evaluate on a benchmark suite that explicitly partitions position-perturbation slices (gold passage at varied ranks) from distractor-density slices, with matched top-k budgets. Run both methods plus their factorial combination (distraction-aware retriever feeding KV-fusion generator) under a unified EM/F1 protocol, and report position-invariance and distractor-robustness metrics separately so each intervention is credited on its native failure mode.

gold_rationale: Both papers address RAG generator behavior under noisy or distractor retrieved contexts and share answer-correctness as the headline metric, so the failure type and problem family genuinely overlap. However, Paper A intervenes at inference-time decoding via a training-free entropy mechanism, while RAFT intervenes via supervised fine-tuning on curated distractor-mixed training data. RAFT additionally targets domain-specific corpora (PubMed, HotpotQA, Gorilla APIs) with CoT plus citation outputs, whereas entropy-based decoding typically targets generic open-domain QA with standard answer outputs, so scope and action policy diverge.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix the same base LLM, retriever, and an evaluation suite spanning both domain-specific corpora (PubMed/Gorilla-style) and open-domain QA (NQ/TriviaQA) under matched distractor ratios. Harmonize the output contract (answer-only vs CoT+citation) and report EM/F1 plus any abstention or citation-faithfulness metrics under a shared action-policy schema, so the training-time and decoding-time interventions are evaluated on identical noise slices.

gold_rationale: Both papers address how LMs handle retrieved context in RAG, so they share a broad problem family. However, Paper A is a diagnostic empirical study profiling retrieval utilization as a function of model scale (no intervention, scale-stratified analysis), while Paper B is a method contribution proposing Early Noise Dropping at the context-preprocessing stage with joint effectiveness plus efficiency metrics. Failure framing differs (general utilization gap vs noise-specific degradation), intervention points differ (none vs early token/passage dropping), and metric targets diverge (scale-conditioned utilization vs denoising accuracy and compute savings). This is a classic method-vs-study mismatch, not a leaderboard pairing.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate END across the same small-to-large model-scale ladder used in Paper A, on overlapping ODQA benchmarks with matched retrievers and top-k, and report retrieval-utilization deltas (e.g., gain from retrieved context, noise-slice accuracy) per scale bucket alongside END's efficiency metrics. Symmetrically, Paper A's utilization probes should be applied to END-denoised contexts to test whether early dropping closes the small-model utilization gap.

gold_rationale: Both works target the same problem family of evaluating end-to-end RAG quality, so failure type and action policy (evaluation-tool role) are aligned. However, MIRAGE is a curated reference-based benchmark with intensive metrics tied to ground-truth annotations across a fixed dataset, while RAGAs is a reference-free LLM-as-judge metric framework (faithfulness, answer relevance, context precision/recall) that runs over arbitrary RAG outputs. The evidence assumption (gold references vs LLM-judge proxies) and the metric definitions differ, so they cannot be placed on a single leaderboard as substitutable systems.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run RAGAs' reference-free metrics on the MIRAGE benchmark dataset and concurrently compute MIRAGE's reference-grounded metrics on the same RAG system outputs, then report agreement (correlation, rank stability) between the two metric families under a fixed retriever and generator. A valid leaderboard comparison would also require harmonizing the unit of evaluation (per-query vs aggregate) and declaring whether judge LLMs are held constant across both protocols.

gold_rationale: Both works contribute to RAG evaluation infrastructure, but they target different pipeline components and failure modes. ReEval is a generator-side hallucination benchmark that perturbs evidence via transferable adversarial attacks and measures hallucination rate under attack. The retrieval-evaluation paper reformulates IR metrics to better reflect downstream LLM utility, targeting retriever-metric misalignment rather than generator robustness. They share the abstract motivation of LLM-aware RAG evaluation, but the intervention point (attack generator vs metric definition), measured quantity, and the artifact being scored differ, so a head-to-head leaderboard is structurally inappropriate.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Place both inside a unified RAG evaluation harness with a fixed retriever and generator, where the retrieval-utility metric from Paper B is computed over evidence sets including ReEval-style adversarial perturbations, and Paper A's hallucination rate is reported jointly with the LLM-aware retrieval scores on the same query distribution. Only then can one ask whether retrieval-quality changes (Paper B) predict adversarial hallucination (Paper A).

gold_rationale: Paper A is a benchmark contribution targeting multi-turn conversational RAG challenges (a specific evaluation setting with its own failure taxonomy and metrics), while Paper B is a modular research framework providing infrastructure to implement and compare RAG algorithms in a unified harness. They occupy complementary roles in the RAG ecosystem rather than competing as substitutable artifacts, and cannot be placed on a shared leaderboard. The benchmark prescribes a multi-turn conversational evaluation protocol; the framework aggregates many methods with its own (largely single-turn) harness and does not itself propose a method or a failure mode.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Reframe as complementary integration rather than head-to-head ranking: instantiate RAGLAB's implemented RAG algorithms (with fixed retriever, generator backbone, and corpus) on the MTRAG-UN benchmark and report under MTRAG-UN's official multi-turn conversational metrics, including any abstention or unanswerable handling. This yields a meaningful leaderboard of RAGLAB methods on MTRAG-UN, but does not make the two papers directly comparable as artifacts.

gold_rationale: Both papers are meta-evaluation contributions for RAG, so they share a broad goal of improving evaluation quality, but they target orthogonal failure modes and intervene at different layers of the evaluation stack. Paper A constructs leakage-free benchmark data to neutralize training-set contamination of robustness scores, while Paper B improves the LLM-as-judge scoring procedure through judge-consistency checks. The interventions (data synthesis vs judge protocol) and headline metrics (robustness on uncontaminated tasks vs judge agreement/accuracy) do not overlap, so they are not substitutable on a single leaderboard, though they are potentially complementary.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Embed both contributions into a shared RAG evaluation harness where Paper A's leakage-free benchmark is the test substrate and Paper B's judge-consistency procedure is the scoring mechanism, then ablate each axis (contaminated vs leakage-free data; standard judge vs consistency-aware judge) on fixed retrievers and generators, reporting both robustness deltas attributable to leakage control and reliability deltas attributable to judge consistency against human-labeled ground truth.

gold_rationale: Both papers target the knowledge-conflict failure mode in RAG and share the assumption that retrieved evidence can contradict itself or parametric knowledge, so the failure family aligns. However, Paper A is a diagnostic study measuring which source (parametric vs retrieved, or across retrieved items) the LLM prefers under conflict, with no proposed intervention, while Paper B is a method paper that intervenes at context assembly via conflict-driven summarization and reports downstream answer trustworthiness/correctness. The roles (analysis vs mitigation), intervention points, and headline metrics diverge, preventing direct leaderboard ranking.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix retriever, generator, and a shared knowledge-conflict benchmark with controlled conflict construction (intra-retrieval and parametric-vs-retrieved); evaluate Paper B's summarization pipeline against an unmodified baseline using Paper A's source-preference diagnostics alongside answer EM/F1 and an explicit abstain option, so the diagnostic preference shifts induced by the intervention can be measured on matched conflict slices.

gold_rationale: Both papers target the same failure mode — context-faithfulness under parametric vs retrieved-context knowledge conflict — and likely share benchmarks like ConFiQA and counterfactual NQ, so failure type and evidence assumption are aligned. However, the intervention points diverge: Context-DPO is a preference-optimization alignment method that retrains the generator on faithful/unfaithful response pairs, while FaithfulRAG performs inference-time fact-level conflict detection and reasoning over self-elicited facts vs context. Action policies (faithful answer generation) overlap but metric bundles likely differ in granularity (response-level MR vs fact-level conflict resolution), preventing a direct leaderboard ranking without harmonization.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix the base LLM backbone (e.g., LLaMA-3 8B, Qwen) and evaluate both methods on a shared benchmark suite including ConFiQA (all three subsets), counterfactual NQ, and a natural-context faithfulness slice; report a unified metric bundle covering memorization ratio, faithfulness rate, and clean-context accuracy under matched conflict-injection protocols. Equalize training budget for Context-DPO and any FaithfulRAG fine-tuning component, and include adaptive baselines so the alignment vs inference-time-reasoning trade-off is isolated.

gold_rationale: Paper A is a position paper arguing that medical RAG systems pose pragmatic and communicative dangers to patient-facing users, with failure modes centered on domain-specific safety, framing, and miscommunication. Paper B is a diagnostic empirical study of positional attention bias (U-shaped performance vs. gold-passage position) in long-context LLMs on multi-doc QA and key-value retrieval. They share no common failure type, evidence setup, intervention, or measurable metric, and one offers normative claims while the other reports controlled behavioral curves. They cannot be placed on a shared leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Comparability would require operationalizing Paper A's medical-communication risks into measurable evaluation slices (e.g., medical QA with patient-safety-graded outputs) and then varying gold-evidence position within long medical contexts to test whether lost-in-the-middle effects amplify the specific communicative harms Paper A enumerates, with shared retriever, generator, and a joint metric bundle covering both positional accuracy and safety-graded communication quality.

gold_rationale: Both papers target the same core failure mode — RALM susceptibility to counterfactual or conflicting retrieved evidence — and both intervene generator-side to make the model less gullible to misleading passages, so failure type and threat assumption align reasonably well. However, KnowPO operates via preference optimization (DPO-style) framed as controllable knowledge selection between parametric and retrieved knowledge, while Paper B targets robustness to counterfactual noise via a different training/inference strategy. Action policies differ (controllable selection vs robust answer generation), and the metric scope likely diverges between conflict-resolution accuracy and noise-robust QA accuracy, preventing a direct leaderboard ranking without harmonization.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix retriever, base generator, and training budget; evaluate both methods on a shared counterfactual-noise benchmark with controlled injection rates (e.g., RGB counterfactual slice plus NQ/TriviaQA with crafted conflicting passages); report a unified metric bundle covering answer accuracy under conflict, parametric-vs-retrieved selection accuracy, and abstention rate under a common action-policy schema.

gold_rationale: Both papers share the surface motif of graph-structured retrieval augmenting an LLM, but they sit in different problem families with non-overlapping evaluation paradigms. Paper A targets hierarchical task planning where the failure mode is unsound or infeasible plans and the intervention couples KG-RAG with symbolic verification, with success measured by plan executability or task completion. Paper B targets graph foundation models where the failure mode is missing graph-domain knowledge and the action is producing predictions on graph learning tasks like node classification or link prediction. There is no shared benchmark or metric on which these systems are substitutable.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared downstream task that both methods can address (for example, KG question answering or graph-grounded reasoning) with a fixed retriever, base LLM, and graph corpus, plus a unified metric that captures both planning correctness and graph-task accuracy under a common action-policy contract. Without such reframing, the two contributions cannot be placed on a common leaderboard.

gold_rationale: Paper A addresses multimodal outside-knowledge VQA with an entity-focused dense retriever evaluated on OK-VQA-style benchmarks, while Paper B is a text-only domain-specific RAG system for Quebec automobile insurance QA. They share only the abstract motif of retrieval-for-QA: modality (image+text vs text), domain corpus, target benchmark, intervention point, and evaluation protocol all diverge. No shared failure mode, evidence assumption, or metric target permits meaningful head-to-head ranking, and neither paper sits in the robustness/security threat-model space the guide emphasizes.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Direct comparison is structurally infeasible across modalities and domains. A valid study would require recasting both as instances of a shared retrieval-augmented QA protocol with matched modality, corpus, retriever backbone, generator, and an aligned answer-quality metric suite, which cannot be constructed across OK-VQA imagery and a Quebec insurance legal corpus.

gold_rationale: Paper A is a text-domain LLM reasoning system that uses knowledge-graph-guided retrieval to improve multi-hop QA faithfulness, while Paper B is a computer-vision image-restoration model that retrieves reference images to ground low-level restoration. The modalities (text vs pixels), failure types (reasoning hallucination vs restoration fidelity), evidence (KG triples and passages vs reference images), metrics (EM/F1/accuracy vs PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS), and output spaces are entirely disjoint. The only shared token is the generic phrase retrieval augmentation, which is insufficient for any common leaderboard or shared harness.
what_valid_comparison_requires: No direct comparison is feasible because the tasks differ in modality and output space. A meaningful comparison would require recasting both under a single multimodal RAG task with shared inputs, retriever, evidence type, and metrics, which is structurally inappropriate for these contributions; at best they could be discussed jointly only as case studies of retrieval augmentation across modalities, not ranked.

gold_rationale: TRACE targets time-series-to-context multimodal embedding for retrieval, optimizing representation alignment and reporting retrieval metrics over a time-series modality. Paper B proposes a unified generative+discriminative training recipe for general vision-language MLLMs, intervening at the training-objective level and reporting downstream MLLM task accuracy. The two share only the loose multimodal umbrella; failure modes, modality scope, intervention point, metric family, and action policy all diverge, so they cannot be placed on a shared leaderboard as substitutable methods.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared multimodal retrieval-augmented MLLM harness with fixed backbone, corpus, and modality coverage (including time series), where one instantiates TRACE as the retriever/embedder and Paper B's training recipe as the generator/discriminator, jointly reporting retrieval quality and downstream task accuracy under matched modality and data budgets.

gold_rationale: Both works sit in the retrieval-augmented generation family and involve chunk/context selection, but they target different problems and are not substitutable. Chunk-Distilled LM intervenes at the generator by distilling retrieved chunks into language modeling (typical metrics: perplexity, generation quality, domain adaptation), while Context Tuning for RAG intervenes upstream on context/tool selection to improve retrieval for downstream task completion (typical metrics: retrieval recall, downstream task accuracy). Failure modes (LM fluency/coverage vs. context/tool retrieval inadequacy) and action policies (token generation vs. context assembly) diverge, so any leaderboard ranking would be apples-to-oranges.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix a shared downstream task (e.g., knowledge-intensive QA or tool-augmented generation), a common retriever, corpus, and generator backbone, then evaluate both methods as alternative pipelines producing the same output under a unified metric bundle (task accuracy plus a retrieval/coverage metric). At minimum, the two approaches must be cast as competing interventions on the same end-to-end objective rather than evaluated in their native, disjoint protocols.

gold_rationale: Both works are generator-side RAG enhancements for QA and likely share answer-correctness metrics on ODQA benchmarks, placing them in the same broad family. However, Paper A targets retriever-generator misalignment via cooperative mutual information exchange and contrastive-layer reranking, while Paper B targets a distinct failure mode of divergent or conflicting views among retrieved passages via a winnowing/filtering mechanism. The intervention points (cross-component cooperation plus reranking vs context filtering) and action policies (rank-then-answer vs filter-then-answer) differ, so a direct leaderboard comparison would conflate two non-equivalent problem framings.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix retriever, generator backbone, and corpus on shared ODQA benchmarks (e.g., NQ, TriviaQA, HotpotQA) and additionally include a conflict-evidence slice (e.g., RGB counterfactual subset or ConflictQA) so both methods can be evaluated on benign and divergent-view conditions. Report EM/F1 plus a conflict-resolution metric and any abstention rate under a unified action-policy contract.

gold_rationale: Both papers improve RAG with a generator-side modification and likely report answer correctness on overlapping ODQA suites (NQ, TriviaQA, PopQA), so they share a problem family. However, RankRAG targets retrieval-ranking quality by instruction-tuning a single LLM to jointly rerank passages and generate answers, while xRAG targets context-length and inference-cost bottlenecks by projecting each retrieved document into a single embedding via a modality bridge. Their failure modes (poor ranking vs. context-length cost), intervention points (training-time unified ranker+generator vs. embedding-level compression with frozen LLM), and primary metric targets (accuracy uplift vs. accuracy-per-token efficiency) diverge, so direct leaderboard ranking is not substitutable.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix the retriever, base LLM backbone, and ODQA benchmark suite, then evaluate both methods under matched compute and context budgets, jointly reporting answer accuracy and efficiency (input tokens, latency, FLOPs). A fair protocol should also test composition (e.g., xRAG-compressed contexts fed to a RankRAG-tuned generator, or RankRAG-reranked passages compressed by xRAG) to separate ranking gains from compression gains.

gold_rationale: Both works target improving RAG quality and likely report answer correctness on overlapping ODQA benchmarks, so they sit in the same problem family. However, SEER intervenes at context assembly via self-aligned evidence extraction (a filter/selector over retrieved passages), while Neuro-RIT intervenes at the generator through neuron-guided instruction tuning aimed at robustness to noisy retrieval. The intervention points and training-vs-inference action policies diverge, and Neuro-RIT's robustness scope (likely including injected distractors) is broader than SEER's extraction-quality scope, precluding a direct leaderboard ranking.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix retriever, base LLM, and a shared benchmark suite (e.g., NQ, TriviaQA, HotpotQA) with a unified noise protocol partitioning irrelevant, distracting, and counterfactual passages at matched rates. Report EM/F1 per noise slice plus a common action policy (answer/abstain), and additionally test composability (SEER-extracted evidence fed into a Neuro-RIT-tuned generator) to disentangle the two intervention points.

gold_rationale: Paper A is a survey/review paper cataloguing security threats, defenses, and benchmarks across the RAG ecosystem under adversarial threat models, while Paper B is the foundational Lewis et al. method paper introducing the RAG architecture for knowledge-intensive NLP tasks (ODQA, fact verification, Jeopardy generation) under benign retrieval. The two artifacts occupy structurally incompatible roles: a security taxonomy versus an original generative-retrieval method, with no shared failure type, no shared metric family (attack success rate and defense coverage vs. EM/F1/accuracy), and no common intervention point. Survey-versus-primary-method comparison cannot yield a head-to-head leaderboard ranking.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A direct comparison is structurally inappropriate. Meaningful engagement would require selecting a specific defense method surveyed in Paper A and benchmarking it against vanilla Lewis-style RAG on a shared corpus, retriever, and generator under a declared threat model, reporting both clean task accuracy (NQ/TriviaQA EM/F1) and adversarial robustness metrics (attack success rate, certified accuracy, abstention) on matched query sets.

gold_rationale: Paper A is a broad survey of RAG architectures, enhancements, and robustness frontiers, while Paper B is a position or perspective piece advocating a denoising-first paradigm for LLM-oriented retrieval. Neither contributes original empirical results, a shared protocol, or a concrete intervention that can be placed on a common leaderboard. Although both touch on retrieval noise and robustness thematically, the artifact types (descriptive survey vs prescriptive perspective) and absence of matched metrics or action policies make direct comparability structurally inappropriate rather than merely partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either reframe both as bibliometric or taxonomic artifacts and compare their coverage of denoising-relevant RAG techniques on a shared inclusion protocol, or compare downstream method instantiations they each recommend on a fixed retriever, generator, noise-injection regime, and metric bundle (answer correctness plus rejection rate) over common ODQA and noise-stress benchmarks.

gold_rationale: Both items are surveys with nearly identical scope — trustworthiness of RAG for LLMs — so failure family and evidence assumptions are tightly aligned and they likely cite overlapping literature on hallucination, robustness, privacy, fairness, and attribution. However, surveys do not propose interventions, do not report empirical metrics, and do not commit to an action policy, so there is no shared leaderboard on which to rank them. Comparability is therefore meaningful only at the taxonomy/coverage level, not as substitutable methods.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Perform a coverage-and-taxonomy alignment: enumerate each survey's top-level trustworthiness dimensions (e.g., robustness, privacy, hallucination, fairness, attribution, safety), map cited works into a shared matrix, and report Jaccard-style coverage overlap per dimension plus divergences in framing, gap analyses, and recommended research agendas. Differences should be reported as scope/emphasis deltas, not as performance rankings.

gold_rationale: Paper A is a security survey/taxonomy cataloging adversarial attacks and defenses on RAG (poisoning, prompt injection, membership inference) under explicit threat models, while Paper B is an inference-efficiency method using retrieval-augmented speculative decoding to accelerate long-context generation under benign conditions. Failure modes (security compromise vs latency/throughput), assumptions (adversarial vs benign), interventions (defense mechanisms vs decoding algorithm), metrics (ASR/defense rate vs tokens-per-second/quality), and action policies (filter/refuse vs accept/reject draft tokens) all diverge. The shared RAG keyword does not create a comparable evaluation surface, and a survey is not directly rankable against a method paper.
what_valid_comparison_requires: No direct comparison is meaningful. At most, Paper A could situate Paper B within its taxonomy by analyzing whether speculative-decoding-based RAG introduces new attack surfaces (e.g., draft-model poisoning, retrieval-timing side channels), which would be a qualitative coverage check rather than a shared leaderboard.

gold_rationale: PoisonedRAG is an offensive contribution that intervenes at the corpus/index via crafted malicious passages and reports attack success rate, while Trust-or-Abstain is a defensive generator-side method whose action policy is selective answering vs abstention. They occupy opposite roles in the attack-defense pipeline so direct leaderboard ranking is inappropriate, but if the self-aware abstention mechanism explicitly covers adversarial/conflicting evidence (not only benign noise) the threat surface aligns enough to evaluate jointly. Role asymmetry plus differing metric targets (ASR vs accuracy+abstention) and intervention points prevent a clean comparison.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Recast both inside a shared attack-defense harness: fix retriever, generator, corpus, and target-question set; instantiate PoisonedRAG (black-box and white-box, with adaptive variants aware of abstention) at matched insertion budgets; evaluate Trust-or-Abstain alongside peer defenses (RobustRAG, Astute RAG) reporting attack success rate, clean accuracy, robust accuracy under attack, abstention/rejection rate, and calibration of the trust signal on poisoned vs clean queries.

gold_rationale: Both works address RAG reliability under imperfect retrieval, so they share a problem family, but their primary failure modes diverge: Paper A is a customizable benchmark instrumenting fine-grained noise types and reporting answer-correctness erosion, while Paper B is an axiomatic analysis arguing existing UE methods violate desirable properties and reports calibration/discrimination-style diagnostics. Artifacts differ in kind (benchmark vs. analytical framework), and action policies differ (answer under noise vs. abstain/score by uncertainty). They are not substitutable on a leaderboard but can be productively coupled.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run the UE methods scrutinized in Paper B on Paper A's Magic Mushroom noise slices using a fixed retriever and generator, jointly reporting EM/F1 alongside UE calibration, selective-prediction AUROC, and abstention rate per noise category. Both works must declare a shared action-policy contract (answer vs. abstain) and matched noise-injection protocols so axiomatic UE failures can be tied to concrete noise-induced answer errors.

gold_rationale: Both papers sit squarely in the robust-RAG family targeting generator behavior under imperfect retrieval and share answer-correctness as a headline metric, so the failure-type axis is genuinely aligned. However, the intervention points diverge: Paper A appears to characterize and mitigate imperfect-retrieval impact (taxonomy plus a training or prompting fix), while RoseRAG specifically applies margin-aware preference optimization (a DPO-style generator update) under an explicit small-scale LLM assumption. This backbone-scale constraint and the preference-optimization machinery are not symmetric to Paper A's setup, and their action policies (abstain vs. answer-only) are unclear and likely mismatched.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix retriever, corpus, and a shared small-scale generator backbone (e.g., LLaMA-2 7B or Mistral 7B); evaluate both methods on a unified imperfect-retrieval protocol that explicitly partitions irrelevant, partially relevant, and counterfactual passages with matched injection rates on shared ODQA benchmarks (NQ/TriviaQA/HotpotQA). Report EM/F1 plus abstention rate under a common action-policy contract, with matched preference-data budgets so the margin-aware DPO step in RoseRAG is not advantaged by training-data asymmetry.

gold_rationale: The two works occupy fundamentally different RAG sub-areas and are not substitutable methods. Paper A tackles hierarchical task planning over a structured knowledge graph with symbolic verification, targeting plan validity for complex multi-step tasks. Paper B is a text-passage rewriting method using a supportiveness criterion for general RALM, targeting answer quality on QA-style benchmarks. Retrieval modality (KG vs text), failure mode (invalid plans vs unsupportive evidence), intervention point (planner plus verifier vs pre-generation rewrite), and evaluation metrics diverge across essentially every coordinate, with no shared benchmark or threat model.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Direct ranking is structurally inappropriate. A meaningful comparison would require fixing a common task family (e.g., multi-hop QA with both a KG and a text corpus), adapting both methods to the same retrieval modality, and reporting a shared metric bundle (answer EM/F1 plus, where relevant, plan-step correctness) on overlapping benchmarks with matched generator backbones.

gold_rationale: Paper A is an offensive security study of indirect prompt injection in deployed LLM systems, with an adversarial threat model where attacker-controlled content reaches the LLM via retrieval; its natural metric is attack feasibility or success across real systems. Paper B is a defensive RL training method that teaches a generator to ground answers and abstain under contextual evidence, with no explicit adversarial threat model and metrics on grounded-answer correctness and abstention quality. The roles (attacker artifact vs trained defender), failure modes (adversarial injection vs benign grounding/insufficiency), threat assumptions, intervention points, and metrics are all misaligned, so direct leaderboard ranking is structurally inappropriate.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Reframe as a shared attack-vs-defense harness: fix retriever, generator backbone, corpus, and query set; instantiate the indirect prompt injection vectors from Paper A (including adaptive variants aware of grounding/abstention) as the adversary; evaluate a GRACE-trained generator alongside other defenses on attack success rate, clean accuracy, grounded accuracy under attack, and abstention rate on injected vs clean queries, under a unified action-policy contract that includes abstention.

gold_rationale: Both papers are defender-side methods that intervene when retrieved sources are problematic, so role and pipeline locus broadly align. However, DRAGged into Conflicts targets inter-source disagreement as a natural-language conflict-detection problem without assuming an adversary, whereas Rescuing the Unpoisoned addresses adversarial corpus poisoning under an explicit threat model with a bounded malicious-insertion budget. Their failure semantics (benign disagreement vs malicious injection), evidence assumptions, and headline metrics (conflict identification and resolution quality vs attack success rate reduction and clean-accuracy preservation) diverge enough to block a direct leaderboard ranking.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix retriever, generator, corpus, and target-query set, then evaluate both methods on a unified harness that includes both natural conflict slices (genuine source disagreement, misinformation in the wild) and adversarial poisoning slices (PoisonedRAG-style injections at matched budgets). Report a joint metric bundle covering answer accuracy, conflict-detection precision/recall, attack success rate, abstention/flag rate, and clean-input utility under a single declared action-policy schema.

gold_rationale: Both papers target reliability of RAG outputs but address fundamentally different sub-problems. RoseRAG mitigates noise-induced answer degradation via generator-side training with margin-aware preference optimization, reporting QA correctness. The faithfulness-UQ paper is a post-hoc detection method that scores whether generated claims are supported by retrieved context, reporting calibration/detection metrics (e.g., AUROC) for fact-checking. They are complementary pipeline stages rather than substitutable methods, so direct leaderboard ranking is inappropriate, though they share the broader trustworthy-RAG family.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix retriever, generator backbone, and a shared benchmark exposing both noisy retrieval and unfaithful-generation cases; evaluate RoseRAG-trained generators under the UQ paper's faithfulness detection harness, and conversely measure whether the UQ scores meaningfully change on RoseRAG outputs. Report a joint bundle: EM/F1 for answer quality plus AUROC/ECE for faithfulness detection under a common action policy (answer, abstain, or flag).

gold_rationale: Paper A is an evaluation-methodology contribution that redefines retrieval metrics to reflect how LLMs consume retrieved evidence, intervening at the metric-design layer with no generator training. Paper B is a language-modeling contribution that distills retrieved chunks into the LM, intervening at the model training and inference layer with perplexity or generation-quality targets. They share only the general retrieval-plus-LLM motif; failure type (metric inadequacy vs LM quality and efficiency), artifact role (evaluator vs trained model), and reported metrics do not align, so head-to-head ranking is structurally inappropriate.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both papers to produce comparable artifacts on a shared task, for instance applying Paper A's redefined retrieval metrics to score the chunk retriever inside Paper B's pipeline, on a common corpus and query set with a fixed generator. Absent that bridging protocol the two contributions cannot be placed on a single leaderboard.

gold_rationale: Both papers aim to improve RAG pipelines but address fundamentally different evidence modalities and intervention points. LI-RAGE targets open-domain table QA with a late-interaction retriever plus explicit signals over structured tables (e.g., NQ-Tables, OTT-QA), whereas DSLR is a post-retrieval document refiner that performs sentence-level re-ranking and reconstruction over unstructured text passages for standard ODQA. The failure modes (table retrieval/grounding vs noisy text passages), evidence assumptions (tables vs prose), intervention points (retriever vs refiner module), and target benchmarks/metrics diverge enough that a direct leaderboard ranking would be misleading.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix a shared backbone generator and a common benchmark family (ideally a hybrid table+text ODQA suite such as OTT-QA, or evaluate DSLR on linearized-table retrieval and LI-RAGE on a text-only ODQA slice) with matched top-k and compute budgets. Then report EM/F1 and answer faithfulness under identical retrieval pools, isolating gains attributable to retrieval-side late interaction vs post-retrieval sentence refinement, and ideally test the two as stackable components rather than substitutes.

gold_rationale: TrustRAG is an adversarial-robustness defense against corpus poisoning (PoisonedRAG-style injection), intervening via clustering and conflict resolution on retrieved passages, with metrics centered on robust accuracy and attack success rate under a malicious threat model. SUGAR is an adaptive retrieval method that uses contextual confidence to gate whether to retrieve at all, targeting unnecessary or harmful retrieval in benign settings. The failure modes, threat models, intervention points (post-retrieval filtering vs retrieval gating), and evaluation metrics do not overlap, so direct head-to-head ranking is structurally inappropriate.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A unified harness fixing retriever, generator, and corpus that evaluates both methods under matched benign and poisoned conditions, reporting clean accuracy, robust accuracy under adversarial injection, retrieval-invocation rate, and abstention. Even then, the role asymmetry (poisoning defense vs adaptive-retrieval gate) means the two should be cast as complementary modules in a stacked pipeline rather than substitutable systems on a single leaderboard.

gold_rationale: Paper A is a diagnostic study of how LLMs negotiate natural parametric-vs-contextual knowledge conflicts in standard RAG, reporting preference/persuasion behaviors on single-passage prompts. Paper B is an offensive contribution that designs adversarial attacks against GraphRAG, a structurally different graph-indexed architecture, and reports attack success metrics under a corpus/graph write-access threat model. The pair simultaneously breaks on role (diagnostic vs attacker), architecture (flat RAG vs GraphRAG), failure type (natural conflict vs poisoning), and metric family, which per pilot rules is not a direct ranking.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix the RAG architecture (both papers evaluated on a common GraphRAG and a common flat-RAG stack) and recast both inside a shared attack-vs-diagnostic harness where GraphRAG under Fire instantiates the adversary with bounded insertion budget and Chameleon/Sloth's conflict taxonomy is measured on the resulting poisoned graphs. Report a joint suite covering attack success rate, parametric-vs-context preference rates, and abstention under matched generator backbones and target-query sets.

gold_rationale: Both works sit in the RAG-robustness family under imperfect retrieval, but they target distinct failure modes and roles. Paper A (ACD) is a decoding-time generator-side method for noisy/irrelevant retrieved passages, optimizing answer correctness on standard QA. Paper B (Know Or Not) is an evaluation library specifically for out-of-knowledge-base queries where the correct action is abstention, with metrics centered on refusal and hallucination rather than EM/F1. Action policies (answer-better vs abstain) and artifact types (method vs benchmark) diverge, so they are not directly rankable.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run ACD inside the Know Or Not harness with a fixed backbone, KB, and retriever, reporting both in-KB answer accuracy and OOKB abstention/hallucination rates under a unified action-policy contract that admits answer, abstain, and filter options. Symmetrically, extend ACD's noisy-context evaluation to include OOKB slices, and benchmark against alternative decoding and abstention baselines.

gold_rationale: Paper A is a benchmark-construction contribution targeting evaluation contamination (test-set leakage) in robust RAG, intervening at dataset generation and reporting leakage and downstream-correctness diagnostics. Paper B is an inference-time method (Superposition Prompting) intervening at prompting/decoding to improve both quality and latency on standard long-context RAG. They share the RAG umbrella but occupy different roles (benchmark artifact vs runtime method), address different failure modes (eval leakage vs distraction/latency), and report different metric bundles, so a direct leaderboard ranking is structurally inappropriate; they can only interact if B is evaluated on A's benchmark.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Treat Paper A as the evaluation harness and run Paper B's Superposition Prompting on Paper A's leakage-free robustness benchmark under a fixed retriever and generator, alongside vanilla RAG and other prompting baselines. Report Paper A's robustness metrics plus end-task EM/F1 and B's latency/throughput so quality, robustness, and efficiency are jointly scored.

gold_rationale: These works share only the RAG acronym and occupy disjoint problem families. RAG-SR augments neural symbolic regression by retrieving candidate sub-expressions to improve equation discovery, with evidence being mathematical primitives and metrics like R-squared or fitness against numerical data. HippoRAG addresses long-term memory and multi-hop QA over text via a Personalized PageRank graph index, with passages as evidence and QA accuracy or F1 as metrics. Failure modes, evidence ontology, intervention point, metrics, and downstream action policies are all incommensurable, so no shared leaderboard ranking is meaningful.
what_valid_comparison_requires: No direct comparison is appropriate. A meaningful evaluation would require a shared task where the same retrieval mechanism could plausibly serve both equation synthesis and textual multi-hop reasoning under one metric, which does not exist here. At most, one could compare retrieval-indexing strategies in isolation on a synthetic benchmark abstracted from both, but that would not constitute a substantive comparability claim about either system.

gold_rationale: GMTP is a security-focused defense that detects adversarially poisoned documents via gradient-based masked token probability, operating under an explicit corpus-poisoning threat model with detection and robust QA metrics. The memory-graph paper is a personalization application that constructs and retrieves over editable user memory graphs, evaluated on personalized agent task quality with no adversarial threat model. The two share only the generic RAG umbrella; failure mode, assumption, intervention point, metric target, and action policy all diverge, so no common leaderboard is meaningful.
what_valid_comparison_requires: These works are not directly comparable. A meaningful comparison would require both methods to be evaluated under a shared task (e.g., poisoned personalization queries over a memory graph) with a unified threat model, fixed retriever/generator, and a joint metric suite covering both poison-detection/robust accuracy and personalization fidelity — which neither paper currently targets.

gold_rationale: Both papers sit in robust RAG and react to problematic retrieved content, but they target fundamentally different failure modes. Paper A handles natural knowledge conflicts (parametric vs retrieved or inter-passage disagreement) via a transparency mechanism under a benign evidence assumption. Paper B defends against adversarial knowledge poisoning using information-flow control inside a multi-agent system under an explicit attacker threat model. Intervention mechanisms, action policies (surface and reconcile vs isolate and block), and headline metrics (conflict resolution accuracy vs attack success rate or certified robustness) diverge, precluding direct leaderboard ranking.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Build a shared harness fixing retriever, generator, and corpus that partitions evidence into natural-conflict and poisoning slices with matched injection budgets; evaluate both methods on both regimes. Report a joint metric bundle (answer accuracy, conflict detection, abstention, attack success rate) under a unified action-policy schema covering answer, surface-conflict, abstain, and isolate options.

gold_rationale: Both works improve RAG end-to-end answer quality, so they share the broad RAG family and likely overlap on answer-correctness metrics. However, the failure modes are orthogonal: Paper A targets robustness against retrieval defects (noisy or irrelevant passages) and intervenes via generator fine-tuning, while SeRTS targets retrieval quality optimization via self-rewarding MCTS-style tree search at retrieval time. Domains also diverge sharply (general ODQA vs biomedical PubMed-style corpora), and the action policies (robust generation under defects vs iterative search-and-refine) are not substitutable on a single leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix retriever, generator backbone, and corpus (ideally run both in a biomedical setting like BioASQ or a general ODQA setting like NQ), then evaluate Paper A's robust fine-tuning and SeRTS's tree search under a shared defect-injection protocol (noisy/irrelevant/counterfactual passages at matched rates) and a shared retrieval-quality protocol, reporting EM/F1 plus retrieval recall and inference cost. Without such matched domain and matched failure-mode partitioning, head-to-head ranking is not meaningful.

gold_rationale: Both works sit inside RAG evaluation, but they target different failure modes and play different roles. Paper A is a detection method for two output-side error types (hallucination and coverage) scoped to controversial topics where multi-perspective coverage is itself a first-class failure. Paper B is a customizable benchmark for input-side retrieval-noise erosion, measuring how perturbed retrieval degrades generation. Hallucination loosely overlaps with noise-induced errors, but coverage error and the controversial-topic scope have no analog in Magic Mushroom, and method-vs-benchmark plus detector-vs-degradation metrics block a direct leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Paper A's hallucination and coverage detectors as a defender on top of Magic Mushroom's controlled noise slices using a shared retriever and generator, reporting detection F1 per noise type and end-to-end answer quality. Symmetrically, extend Magic Mushroom with a controversial-topics partition and a coverage-error noise category so both papers report on a common failure taxonomy and metric bundle.

gold_rationale: Paper A is a domain-specific text-to-SQL application that retrieves schema/exemplar context to generate executable SQL over EHR databases for epidemiology questions, with success measured by SQL execution accuracy against structured medical records. Paper B is a general-purpose robust-RAG method that uses neuron-guided instruction tuning of the generator to resist noisy or distracting retrieved passages, evaluated as free-text QA. The output spaces (SQL vs natural language), failure modes (schema/query-generation errors vs passage-noise distraction), evidence sources (structured EHR tables vs unstructured text corpora), and metrics (execution accuracy vs EM/F1 under noise) are non-substitutable. They share only the high-level label retrieval-augmented.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Direct comparison is not reconstructible on a common leaderboard. At minimum one would need a shared task formulation (either text-to-SQL over the same EHR benchmark with matched retrievers and SQL execution metrics, or unstructured QA with matched noise-injection protocols), the same backbone LLM, and a common action policy, none of which the two papers jointly support.

gold_rationale: Paper A is an offensive security contribution that crafts coordinated prompt and corpus-injection attacks on RAG via bilevel optimization under an explicit adversarial threat model, measured by attack success rate. Paper B is a benign capability/efficiency study comparing RAG pipelines against long-context LLMs and proposing a hybrid routing approach, measured by answer quality on long-context QA/summarization benchmarks. They share only the RAG substrate; failure mode (adversarial corruption vs architecture choice tradeoff), evidence assumption (attacker-controlled vs clean corpus), intervention point, metric target, and action policy all diverge, so no direct leaderboard ranking is meaningful.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared evaluation would require recasting Paper B's RAG vs long-context comparison inside an adversarial harness where PR-Attack (and baselines) inject malicious passages against both the RAG and long-context configurations under matched insertion budgets, then jointly reporting clean answer quality and attack success rate per architecture. Without overlaying a common threat model and metric bundle, the two works address unrelated questions.

gold_rationale: Paper A is a defensive/diagnostic contribution that probes the generator's latent representations to improve faithfulness to retrieved context, implicitly under benign or naturally noisy retrieval. Paper B is an offensive black-box attack that crafts adversarial queries and passages to manipulate opinions expressed by RAG, intervening at the retrieval/corpus side under an explicit adversarial threat model. The two occupy opposite roles in the attack-defense pipeline, with mismatched failure modes (faithfulness drift vs. opinion manipulation), metrics (faithfulness scores vs. opinion-shift / attack success), and evidence assumptions, so they cannot share a leaderboard as substitutable systems.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Recast as a shared attack-defense harness: fix retriever, generator, corpus, and opinion-target query set; instantiate FlippedRAG as the adversary with matched insertion budgets, and evaluate the latent-probing method as a detector or faithfulness-enforcing defense alongside baselines such as RobustRAG and perplexity filtering. Report opinion-shift rate, detection AUC, clean-task faithfulness, and abstention under a unified action-policy schema.

gold_rationale: Paper A is a language-modeling method that integrates retrieved text chunks into generation via a distillation-style mechanism, evaluated primarily on LM quality/efficiency. Paper B is a diagnostic/behavioral study of when search-augmented LLMs issue unnecessary retrieval calls, focused on QA accuracy and search-decision policy. The two works do not share a failure mode (LM generation quality vs. over-triggered search), intervene at different stages (chunk-conditioned LM head vs. search-trigger control), and report incommensurable metrics. They are not substitutable methods on any common leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared evaluation harness with a fixed retriever and base LLM where both works are framed under an explicit search/no-search action policy, evaluated on overlapping QA benchmarks with matched search-budget settings, and reporting a unified bundle (answer accuracy, retrieval calls per query, latency, and LM perplexity on the same corpus). Without that, only loose thematic overlap exists.

gold_rationale: Both papers share the loose RAG-robustness framing, but they target fundamentally different failure modes: Paper A diagnoses cross-lingual and culturally-sensitive inconsistency under a multilingual evidence assumption, while Paper B targets retrieval defects (noisy/irrelevant passages) under a typically monolingual ODQA setup. There is also a role asymmetry — Paper A is a benchmark contribution, Paper B is a generator-side fine-tuning method — so they cannot be placed on a shared leaderboard. Comparability exists only at the abstract umbrella of robust RAG.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Apply Paper B's robust fine-tuning recipe to Paper A's multilingual culturally-sensitive benchmark using matched retrievers and multilingual generator backbones, reporting cross-lingual robustness slices alongside standard EM/F1 on retrieval-defect partitions. Symmetrically, extend Paper A's benchmark with explicit retrieval-defect injection (irrelevant, counterfactual) so both methods can be scored on a unified slice schema with a common action policy.

gold_rationale: Paper A is a multi-modal LLM training methodology contribution that unifies generative and discriminative objectives for vision-language tasks, while Paper B is a text-only RAG inference acceleration method that prunes context tokens to reduce latency. They share no common failure mode (MLLM capability gaps vs RAG inference cost), no common evidence regime (image-text pairs vs retrieved passages), no common intervention point (training objective design vs inference-time context selection), and no common metric target (MLLM benchmarks vs throughput/accuracy tradeoff). The only superficial link is that both involve large language models, which is far too broad to ground a direct comparison.
what_valid_comparison_requires: No meaningful direct comparison is possible because the works inhabit disjoint problem families. A valid comparability claim would require both papers to address the same failure (e.g., both attacking RAG inference cost, or both targeting MLLM training) on a shared task, backbone, and metric suite, which is not the case here.

gold_rationale: CPA-RAG is an offensive contribution that intervenes at the corpus by injecting covertly crafted poisoned passages under an adversarial threat model and reports attack success rate. Divide-Then-Align is a defensive alignment method that fine-tunes the generator to honor epistemic knowledge boundaries on naturally retrieved evidence and reports honesty, accuracy, and abstention. The failure modes (adversarial integrity attack vs natural knowledge-gap miscalibration), threat models, intervention points, metrics, and action policies all diverge, so they cannot share a leaderboard as substitutable methods.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Reframe inside a shared attack-defense harness with fixed retriever, generator, corpus, and query set; instantiate CPA-RAG as the adversary at controlled insertion budgets and evaluate Divide-Then-Align (alongside defenses like RobustRAG or Astute RAG) on the resulting poisoned corpora; report a unified bundle of attack success rate, honest abstention rate under clean and poisoned contexts, and answer accuracy.

gold_rationale: Paper A is a defensive interpretability-plus-mitigation work on natural parametric-vs-context knowledge conflicts in standard LMs, intervening at model internals (attention head pruning) and reporting conflict-resolution accuracy with no adversary in the threat model. Paper B is an offensive poisoning attack on graph-based RAG, intervening at the knowledge-graph corpus under an explicit adversarial threat model and reporting attack success rate. Roles (defender vs attacker), target systems (vanilla LM/RAG vs GraphRAG), and metrics are structurally asymmetric, so they cannot share a leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Embed both inside a unified attack-vs-defense harness on a shared GraphRAG stack: instantiate Paper B's graph poisoning as the adversary with matched insertion budgets, then apply Paper A's head-level mitigation as one defense alongside other baselines. Jointly report attack success rate, clean accuracy, post-defense robust accuracy, and any abstention behavior on the same query set and graph corpus.

gold_rationale: Both sit under the RAG umbrella and could in principle share KILT/ODQA benchmarks, but they target orthogonal concerns. FiD-Light is an efficiency contribution that compresses encoder-to-decoder representations in the Fusion-in-Decoder architecture, optimizing the latency/quality frontier with an always-answer policy. SURE-RAG is a reliability contribution that intervenes at evidence verification with sufficiency and uncertainty estimates, supporting selective answering or abstention. Failure target, intervention point, metric bundle, and action policy all diverge, so direct leaderboard ranking is inappropriate even though task overlap exists.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix a shared generator backbone, retriever, and benchmark suite (e.g., KILT or NQ/TriviaQA/HotpotQA), and evaluate both systems under a unified contract that jointly reports answer quality, latency/throughput, and abstention/calibration metrics. Either equip FiD-Light with a comparable selective-answering head or measure SURE-RAG's efficiency overhead, so both can be placed on a joint quality-efficiency-reliability frontier rather than compared on a single axis.

gold_rationale: Both works touch retrieval for QA, but they are structurally different artifacts. Paper A is a 2025 shared-task venue that fixes a web-scale corpus (Fineweb) and a specified LLM, soliciting heterogeneous end-to-end RAG submissions scored on overall answer quality. Paper B is a 2019 retrieval-method paper proposing a specific multi-hop paragraph retriever evaluated on Wikipedia-based multi-hop QA (e.g., HotpotQA) with retrieval-centric metrics. The role mismatch (challenge venue vs single method), corpus/domain mismatch, and metric scope (end-to-end RAG quality vs retrieval recall) prevent direct ranking, though both share the broad retrieval-for-QA failure family.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Submit Paper B's multi-hop retriever as a LiveRAG entry under the challenge's fixed corpus, generator, and evaluation harness, or conversely re-run LiveRAG top systems on a multi-hop Wikipedia benchmark with matched top-k and retrieval/end-to-end metrics. Comparability also requires harmonizing single-hop vs multi-hop query mixes and reporting both retrieval recall and answer-correctness on the same query set.
